results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  Generally, you should keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  For property, keep records relating to the asset until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

You need to keep business records for several key reasons:

1. **To prepare accurate tax returns.**  
   Business records must support the income, expenses, and credits you report on your tax filings [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

2. **To facilitate dealings with banks and creditors.**

3. **To satisfy IRS inspection requirements.**  
   The IRS may request that you explain the items reported on your returns. 4. **To validate the entries in your books and tax return.**

5. **Because of the IRS’s retention rules.**  
   You must keep records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code, meaning for the duration required by tax law [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.**  


**STEP 2.**  
The IRS requires you to keep business records for the length of time the records may be needed for tax‑administration purposes. In most cases that is the period of limitation for the tax return on which the records support an item of income or deduction; for employment taxes it is a separate requirement.

* General rule – keep all records that support the items on a tax return until the period of limitation for that return expires (or longer if required for other reasons). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* Period‑of‑limitations table (Table 3, “Period of Limitations”) shows the specific durations:  
  * 3 years after the return is filed for most returns, including the ordinary right to amend and the period the IRS can assess additional tax.  
  * 6 years if you fail to report **more than 25 % of the gross income shown on the return**.  
  * No limitation (“not limited”) for a fraudulent return. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
* Employment‑tax records must be kept for **4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
* Records relating to property (for depreciation, amortization, basis, gain/loss at disposition) should be kept until the period of limitation expires for the year in which the property is disposed of. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

Thus, unless a longer period is required for another purpose (e.g., insurance or creditor needs), you should keep tax records for at least 3 years (6 years for large under‑reporting cases), 4 years for employment‑tax records, and until the property‑disposition limitation period for asset‑related records.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**USING:** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Answer**

When you file your first business tax return you must pick an accounting method that matches how you keep records and how you handle revenue and expenses.

* **Cash method** – Record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them.  
  *This method is generally the simplest and is preferred when the business has no inventory.*  
  *If your business is a small‑business taxpayer that does *not* need to keep inventory, you may use the cash method even if you have some inventoriable items that are treated as non‑incidental materials or supplies* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

* **Accrual method** – Record income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands.  
  *If your business sells or manufactures inventory, you must use the accrual method for purchases and sales unless you qualify for the small‑business exception* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

* **Combination or special methods** – You may combine elements of cash and accrual methods, or use special methods for particular items, provided the overall system clearly shows your income and is used consistently.  
  *For example, you can use the cash method for all non‑inventory items while treating inventory under an accrual method* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

So, if your business has no inventory and qualifies as a small‑business taxpayer, the cash method is usually appropriate; otherwise default to the accrual method (or a permissible combination).



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**STEP 1. Passages that actually answer the question**


---

**STEP 2. Answer**

1. **Choose a legal structure for the business** – Before filing tax forms you must decide whether you will operate as a sole‑proprietorship, partnership, corporation or limited‑liability company (IRS Publication 583, page 1).

2. **Obtain a taxpayer identification number (TIN)** – Apply for an employer identification number (EIN) if you are not a sole proprietor or if you plan to hire employees. The EIN can be obtained quickly online, by fax, mail or telephone (IRS Publication 583, page 4).  
   - *“You must have a TIN… two of the most common kinds of TINs are the social security number (SSN) and the employer identification number (EIN).”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

3. **Select your tax year and accounting method** – Decide whether you will use a calendar or fiscal year. Establish your accounting method (cash or accrual) when you file your first income‑tax return (IRS Publication 583, pages 5‑5).  
   - *“You must decide… whether you will use a calendar tax year or a fiscal tax year… choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

4. **Set up a bookkeeping system** – Pick a single‑entry or double‑entry system. Keep separate ledgers or journals and, if using a computer package, produce records that are legible and can be reproduced (IRS Publication 583, page 15).  
   - *“You must decide whether to use a single‑entry or a double‑entry bookkeeping system.”* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

5. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – Label each deposit and payment with its source, and keep the checkbook as the primary source of transaction data. Reconcile the account monthly to keep your books accurate (IRS Publication 583, page 14).  
   - *“One of the first things you should do when you start a business is open a business checking account… Reconcile the checking account each month.”* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

6. **Keep supporting documents for every transaction** – Keep receipts, invoices, bank statements, canceled checks and other records that support the entries in your books. Store them in an orderly, safe place and keep them for the period required by the IRS (IRS Publication 583, page 12).  
   - *“Supporting documents include sales slips, paid bills, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, and canceled checks… Keep them in an orderly fashion and in a safe place.”* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

7. **Maintain records according to IRS rules** – Use an electronic storage system that preserves, indexes and reproduces your books in a legible format if you transition from paper. Keep records for the statutory limitation period (IRS Publication 583, page 12).  
   - *“All requirements that apply to hard copy books and records also apply to electronic storage systems… You must keep the electronic storage system for as long as it is material to the administration of tax law.”* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

By following these steps—choosing a structure, obtaining an EIN, setting a tax year and accounting method, establishing a reliable bookkeeping system, separating personal and business funds, and retaining all supporting documentation—you begin a business and keep your taxes organized in a manner that satisfies IRS requirements.

runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14), [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

---

**STEP 2 – Answer**

**1. Writing a business plan**

*Structure* – The SBA guide describes a typical outline that covers the major sections any business plan should contain:  
- Cover page, table of contents, executive summary, description of the business, management plan, market analysis, marketing strategy, product/service description, facilities and equipment, operational needs, cost of barriers, and exhibits [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  

*Content* – Each section should be filled out as follows:  
- **Executive summary** – a brief two‑paragraph overview that states the idea, capital needed, use of funds, and a short schedule of goals [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
- **Business description** – explain the industry, competitive advantage, history, status, and projected growth [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  
- **Product/Service** – detail what you sell, why it matters, uniqueness, future plans, and manufacturing process if applicable [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  
- **Market and marketing** – identify your target market, estimate its size, list competitors, and describe the sales and promotion methods you will use [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14).  
- **Operations** – describe facilities, equipment, production capacity, and logistical support [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  
- **Management** – show ownership, board, day‑to‑day manager, and accounting responsibilities [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13).  
- **Financial section** – include a sources‑and‑uses of funds statement, a three‑year income projection, a cash‑flow projection, a balance sheet, and a break‑even analysis [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  

**2. Setting up accounting**

*Choose an accounting method* – When filing your first return you must pick either the cash method or the accrual method [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
- **Cash method**: record income when received and expenses when paid.  
- **Accrual method**: record income when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash flow.  

*Record‑keeping system* – Decide between a single‑entry or a double‑entry bookkeeping system [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).  
- **Single‑entry**: simple income‑statement‑based system with daily cash receipts and monthly summaries.  
- **Double‑entry**: uses journals and ledgers; each transaction has a debit and a credit, and balances must equal [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).  

*Business checkbook* – Open a separate business checking account. Deposit all receipts, reconcile monthly, and keep a daily register; keep supporting documents such as deposit slips, canceled checks, and receipts [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  

*Supporting documents* – Keep receipts, invoices, deposit slips, and canceled checks for all sales and expenses. Organize them by year and type; they support the entries in your books and your tax return [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13).  

*Electronic records* – An electronic system must store, index, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce the original hard‑copy records, and must be able to provide the IRS with a legible copy [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).  

**Summary**

Use the SBA guide to build a comprehensive business plan that includes executive summary, market analysis, operations, management, and a robust financial section. Simultaneously, apply the IRS guidance to select an appropriate accounting method (cash or accrual), set up either a single‑ or double‑entry record‑keeping system, maintain a separate business checkbook with monthly reconciliations, and preserve all supporting documents, whether on paper or electronically, in a system that the IRS can audit if needed.

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
**Step 1 – Passages that answer the question**


**Step 2 – Answer**

You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **To identify and separate income sources** – Records show where your receipts come from and help you distinguish business receipts from non‑business or non‑taxable income, enabling correct reporting to the IRS. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **To track deductible expenses** – Because many business expenses may be forgotten if not recorded when incurred, maintaining records ensures you can claim legitimate deductions on your tax return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **To prepare accurate tax returns** – Good records provide the data necessary to report income, expenses, and credits, and they are the same documents you use for monitoring your business and creating financial statements. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **To support items reported on your tax returns** – The IRS can request explanation or proof of any reported item; a complete record set speeds up any examination and reduces the risk of penalties. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **To meet legal retention requirements** – You must keep records for the period that the Internal Revenue Code could allow the IRS to assess additional tax or for you to amend a return. Generally, that is until the limitations period expires for that tax year (typically three to six years, depending on the item). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

6. **To maintain a reliable supporting system** – Your record‑keeping system (ebooks, ledgers, electronic files) must preserve supporting documents such as invoices, receipts, bank statements, and cancelled checks because they substantiate entries in your books and tax filings. runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.**  


---

**STEP 2.**  
The IRS states that you choose an accounting method when you file your first income‐tax return for the business.  
There are two basic methods:

* **Cash method** – Income is reported when you receive it, and expenses are generally deducted when you pay them. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
* **Accrual method** – Income is reported when you earn it, and expenses are reported when you incur them, regardless of when payment is made. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

If your business **does not keep inventory**, the cash method is typically the simplest and is often recommended for many sole proprietors and small businesses. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

If your business **must keep inventory** (i.e., you sell, produce, or purchase merchandise), you are required to use an accrual method for purchases and sales, even if you otherwise prefer the cash method, unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer who may treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

You may also use a **combination method** that blends cash and accrual elements, but all items that are treated as income or expense must be consistent, and if an inventory exists the accrual method must be used for that portion. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

Finally, once a method is chosen you must apply it consistently to both the calculation of taxable income and to your bookkeeping; changing the method later requires IRS approval. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

**STEP 2**  

**Tax records to keep**  
- Every business must retain “supporting documents” that prove the income and expenses reported on the tax return.  These include sales slips, paid bills, invoices, receipts, bank deposit slips, canceled checks, and payroll records.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- If the business owns property, record all information needed to compute depreciation, amortization, or a gain/loss on disposition: the date and method of acquisition, purchase price, cost of improvements, Section 179 deduction taken, usage, disposal date, and proceeds.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

**How long to keep tax records**  
- Keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return until the period of limitation for that return expires; the general limitation is three years from the due date of the return (or from the due date plus extensions).  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for at least four years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- Keep records related to any property until the period of limitation expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition, because they are needed to calculate depreciation or gain/loss at that time.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- Retain copies of your filed tax returns (including amended returns) because they are helpful for future tax calculations and for any IRS audit.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Injury and illness records to keep**  
- Maintain OSHA Form 300 (Injury/Illness Log), Form 301 (Incident Report), and Form 300A (Summary) at the worksite.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- Keep records of worker medical treatment and employee exposure that are required for each specific type of record (e.g., medical records, exposure monitoring data).  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- Preserve worker training records that are required by OSHA standards and keep them accessible to workers.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

**How long to keep injury and illness records**  
- The OSHA injury/illness logs (Form 300/300A/301) must be kept at the worksite for at least five years.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- Worker medical and exposure records are retained for the time period required for each specific type of record, as specified by OSHA regulations.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- (Employees’ training records) are kept for the duration required by the applicable OSHA standard.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

In summary, keep detailed invoices, receipts, payroll, and other supporting documents for tax purposes, and retain them for the period of limitation (usually 3‑4 years, longer for certain assets).  For work‑related injuries and illnesses, keep the OSHA logs and related medical/vendor records on site for no less than five years, with special retention periods set by OSHA for medical and training documents.

[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15), [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)

**STEP 2**  

**Keeping employees safe**

1. **Create a safety‑and‑health program** that includes management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification and assessment, hazard prevention and control, education and training, program evaluation, and communication .  
2. **Conduct regular workplace inspections** to identify and eliminate hazards, and keep records of findings and corrective actions .  
3. **Provide ergonomics training** and address musculoskeletal‑disorder risks through engineering, administrative, and protective‑equipment controls .  
4. **Use OSHA On‑Site Consultation** for free, confidential hazard identification, compliance guidance, and training support .  

**Keeping the premises accessible**

1. **Identify and remove physical barriers** that prevent people with disabilities from entering, moving through, or using your facility [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7).  
2. **Provide an accessible entrance**: a single step can be mitigated by an alternate entrance, a short ramp, or a lift; when multiple entrances exist, at least one must be accessible and a sign must direct customers to it [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
3. **Install ramps with a slope no steeper than 1:12** and handrails whenever the rise is greater than 6 inches [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
4. **Ensure accessible parking**: spaces must be at least 8 ft wide, have a 98‑in clearance, an access aisle, and a sign with the international symbol of accessibility [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
5. **Make sales and service counters accessible**: at least a 36‑in long section no higher than 36 in above the floor, with a clear floor space of at least 30 × 48 in in front of it [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
6. **Comply with the ADA Standards for Accessible Design** for all new construction (after 1/26/1993) and for all alterations (after 1/26/1992) [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19).  
7. **Seek technical assistance** from the DOJ ADA Information Line, DBTACs, or the Access Board, and take advantage of available tax credits and deductions for barrier‑removal work [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19).

runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that directly answer the question**

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14), [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

---

**STEP 2 – Answer**

**1. Writing a business plan**

A business plan is organized around a clear outline so that you can gather, evaluate, and present all the information a potential investor or lender will need.

- Begin with a **Cover Page** containing the company name, address, phone number, owners, and the date of the plan [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
- File a **Table of Contents** (optional).  
- Write an **Executive Summary** that gives a concise overview of the idea, the amount of capital needed, how it will be used, and a brief schedule of goals [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
- In the **Business** section, describe the industry, the competitive advantage, operating plan, and relevant regulations [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  
- Include a **Management** plan that lists owners, their ownership percentages, day‑to‑day managers, and key advisors [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  
- Provide a **Market** analysis that identifies the target market, competition, and marketing strategy [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  
- In **Money** (the financial section), attach the key documents that lenders require:  
  * Summary of Financial Need,  
  * 3‑Year Income Projection,  
  * Cash‑Flow Projection,  
  * Balance Sheet,  
  * Break‑Even Analysis [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).  
- List all **Exhibits** that support the facts in the plan, such as resumes, purchase agreements, contracts, etc. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

**2. Setting up accounting**

You must choose an accounting method, establish a bookkeeping system, and keep proper records.

- **Choose an accounting method** when you file your first tax return. The two main methods are:
  * *Cash method*: income is reported when received and expenses are deducted when paid.  
  * *Accrual method*: income is reported when earned and expenses are deducted when incurred, regardless of cash dates.  
  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

- **Set up a bookkeeping system**. You can use:

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.  Passages that provide the answer**


---

**STEP 2.  Answer**

You must keep records that support any item of income or deduction on a return **until that return’s period of limitation runs out** (IRS Pub. 583, page 16).  The standard period of limitation is three years, but some situations require longer: if you omit income that is more than 25 % of the gross income shown on the return the limitation is six years, and a fraudulent return is not limited (IRS Pub. 583, page 15).

In addition:

* Keep copies of your filed tax returns for the same period of limitation, so you can reference them when preparing future returns or amended returns (IRS Pub. 583, page 16).

* If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for **at least four years after the tax becomes due or is paid**, whichever is later (IRS Pub. 583, page 16).

* Keep records relating to any property you own until the period of limitation expires for the year in which you dispose of that property.  These records are needed to calculate depreciation, amortization, or any gain or loss when you sell or otherwise dispose of the property (IRS Pub. 583, page 16).

* When records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you confirm that no other law (e.g., insurance or creditor requirements) requires you to keep them longer (IRS Pub. 583, page 16).

Good records are needed to prepare the return and to prove the amounts when the IRS examines them [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**USING:**  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15),  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14),  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14),  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Answer**

You can choose one of two basic accounting methods when you file your first income‑tax return: a **cash method** or an **accrual method** (you may also use a combination, but see the restrictions below) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).

- **Cash method** – You report income in the year you actually receive it and, generally, deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them. This method is simpler and is the default for most individuals and many sole proprietors who do not keep inventory [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).  

- **Accrual method** – You report income in the year you earn it, irrespective of when payment is received, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, regardless of when they are paid [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).

Which method you should use depends mainly on whether your business maintains inventory:

- If your business **does not need an inventory** to account for its income (for example, a service‑only business, or a business that sells only intangible products), you may use the **cash method** and find it easier to keep records [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

- If your business **requires inventory** (i.e., you produce, purchase, or sell merchandise as part of normal business activity), you **must generally** use the **accrual method** for inventory purchases and sales, unless you qualify as a “small business taxpayer” and meet the special rules that allow you to avoid keeping inventory while still using a method that clearly reflects income [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

  *Small‑business taxpayers* may choose to forego maintaining an inventory **and** can use an accounting method that treats inventories as non‑incidental material or supplies, or that conforms to your financial accounting treatment, thereby satisfying the “clearly reflects income” requirement [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

**Summary**  

1. **No inventory → Cash method** (simplest and most common for small businesses).  
2. **Inventory required → Accrual method** (unless you qualify as a small business taxpayer and can apply the special inventory exception).  

After you file your first return with a chosen method, you can only change it with IRS approval (using Form 1128).

runs.answer:

**What to track for taxes**

* Keep a complete set of supporting documents for every transaction that shows the amount and source of each income receipt—for example, cash‑register tapes, bank deposit slips, receipt books, and sales invoices [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).  
* Record all business expenses in your books and keep receipts or other proof of each expense.  These should include categories such as depreciation, lease payments, registration, insurance, repairs, gas, and other vehicle‑related costs [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  
* Track the actual business mileage when you use a vehicle for both business and personal purposes, and calculate the deductible portion as the ratio of business miles to total miles [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  
* Maintain payroll records if you pay employees, and keep records of federal income tax withholding, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and unemployment tax remittances [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13).  
* Record any estimated tax payments you make during the year, and keep receipts or bank statements confirming the amount and date of each payment [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).  

**What to track for travel expenses**

* Log every business trip with the date, destination, purpose, and the amount of time you were away from your tax home [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).

* Track lodging costs and meals while on a business trip; you can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if the trip is overnight or long enough that you need to sleep or rest [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41). You need to keep business records for several key reasons:

   Business records must support the income, expenses, and credits you report on your tax filings [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

2. **To facilitate dealings with banks and creditors.**  
   Good records can help you satisfy the information needs of lenders and other creditors, improving your ability to secure financing [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

3. **To satisfy IRS inspection requirements.**  
   The IRS may request that you explain the items reported on your returns. Having a complete, readily available set of records speeds up any examination and ensures you can comply with IRS inquiries [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

4. **To validate the entries in your books and tax return.**

5. **Because of the IRS’s retention rules.**  
   You must keep records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code, meaning for the duration required by tax law [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
**USING:** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

You are partially exempt from OSHA’s injury and illness record‑keeping requirements if you meet **either** of the following conditions (29 CFR 1904.1):

* **You had 10 or fewer workers during every month of the last calendar year**, or  
* **Your business is in a low‑hazard industry listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A**.

Even when you are exempt from keeping a Form 300 log, you must still report

* All work‑related fatalities,  
* All work‑related in‑patient hospitalizations,  
* All amputations, and  
* All loss‑of‑an‑eye cases  

to OSHA within the required time frames (within 8 hours for fatalities, within 24 hours for the others).  

If your workplace does not meet the exemption criteria, you must keep the OSHA injury and illness records (Form 300, Form 301, and the annual Form 300A summary) and retain them at the worksite for at least five years.
